Right to Be Forgotten Damages and Sanctions in Italy

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Right to be forgotten damages can be claimed in Italy when a search engine, publisher or other data controller keeps processing your personal data unlawfully after you were entitled to erasure or delisting, and that processing caused you real harm. Compensation comes from the civil courts under Article 82 GDPR, while fines imposed by the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali are public sanctions paid to the State. The two paths have different goals, different evidence requirements and cannot always be pursued together.

When a violation of the right to be forgotten becomes compensable

Compensation is due when three elements coexist: an infringement of data protection law, a damage suffered by you, and a causal link between the two. The mere presence of an old article in search results is not an infringement; the infringement usually begins when a controller refuses or ignores a well-founded request for erasure or delisting and continues to process the data.

Typical situations include a search engine that keeps showing an outdated news story after a request that clearly met the criteria, a newspaper that refuses to update or anonymise an archive article about an acquitted person, or a directory that continues to publish personal details after a valid erasure request under Article 17 GDPR. The substantive conditions for delisting are covered in our article on what the right to be forgotten can remove from Google; here we look at the consequences when those conditions are ignored.

Compensation under Article 82 GDPR in Italian courts

Article 82 GDPR gives anyone who has suffered material or non-material damage from an infringement the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor responsible. The controller escapes liability only by proving that it is not in any way responsible for the event that caused the damage.

Material and non-material damage

Material damage covers measurable economic losses: a contract not signed, a job offer withdrawn, clients lost by a professional in Turin or Naples after they found the old story. Non-material damage covers distress, damage to reputation and the impact on personal and family life, which Italian courts assess under art. 2059 of the Civil Code. The EU Court of Justice has clarified that an infringement alone does not automatically give rise to compensation, but also that there is no minimum seriousness threshold under EU law; the person must still prove that some damage actually occurred.

Where and how to file

Data protection disputes are heard by the ordinary court (tribunale) of the place where the controller resides or, in many cases, where the data subject lives, under the procedure referred to in the Codice Privacy. A civil claim can request both compensation and an order to delist or erase, which makes it a powerful tool when the controller has already refused. The general limitation period for non-contractual liability in Italy is five years, but delay weakens a claim in practice because evidence of harm becomes harder to collect.

Garante sanctions and GDPR right to be forgotten penalties

The Garante can order a controller to delist or erase data and can impose administrative fines, but those fines do not compensate the individual. GDPR right to be forgotten penalties fall under Article 83, which allows fines of up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for breaches of data subject rights.

In practice, a complaint (reclamo) to the Garante under Article 77 GDPR is the faster and cheaper route when the main goal is to make the content disappear. The authority examines the case, can ask the controller for explanations and can issue binding orders. Its corrective powers under Article 58 include:

  • warnings and reprimands addressed to the controller;
  • orders to comply with the erasure or delisting request within a set deadline;
  • temporary or definitive limitations on the processing;
  • administrative fines, decided case by case according to the nature and duration of the breach, intent or negligence and the steps taken to mitigate harm.
A Garante decision makes the content disappear; a court judgment can also make someone pay for the harm it caused. Choose according to what you actually need.

Choosing between a complaint and a lawsuit

Italian law treats the complaint to the Garante and the court action as alternatives for the same claim between the same parties: under art. 140-bis of the Codice Privacy, bringing the dispute before the court prevents a complaint on the same subject, and a pending complaint limits a later court action on the same object. The choice must therefore be made deliberately at the start.

AspectComplaint to the GaranteCivil action in court
Main outcomeOrder to delist or erase, possible fineOrder plus compensation
CostLow, no lawyer strictly requiredLegal fees and court costs
Who receives moneyThe State (fines)The injured person
Evidence of harmNot essential for the orderEssential for damages

A common sequence is to request delisting first, then file a complaint if it is refused, and evaluate a separate damages claim only when the harm is significant and well documented. The way Google handles delisting before any dispute arises is described in our article on the deindexing mechanism and its limits.

Evidence of harm you will need

Courts award compensation only for damage that is proven, so the claim stands or falls on documentation gathered from the moment the problem appears. Italian judges look for concrete proof of how the persistent result affected your life or work, not general statements about anxiety or embarrassment.

  • Dated, certified captures of the search results showing the content under your name, preferably acquired with forensic methods that record hash values and timestamps.
  • The full correspondence with the controller: your request, the reply or silence, and any reminders.
  • Documents linking the result to specific losses, such as emails ending negotiations, rejected applications or a bank's refusal referring to the information found online.
  • Accounting data showing a drop in revenue for professionals and businesses, with a timeline matching the visibility of the content.
  • Medical or psychological reports and witness statements for non-material damage to health and relationships.

Evidence of the controller's conduct also matters. A refusal that ignored a court acquittal or a Riforma Cartabia annotation (art. 64-ter disp. att. c.p.p.) shows negligence much more clearly than a borderline case where reasonable people could disagree.

Other right to be forgotten sanctions and limits

Beyond fines and damages, right to be forgotten sanctions can include criminal liability in serious cases. Art. 167 of the Codice Privacy punishes unlawful processing carried out to obtain a profit or to cause harm, when it results in damage to the person concerned; it is reserved for deliberate conduct rather than a mistaken assessment of a delisting request.

Realistic expectations are important. Many disputes end once the content is delisted, and awards for non-material damage in Italy are generally measured rather than punitive.
